Rough solutions of the Einstein-Vacuum equations

Sergiu Klainerman Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton NJ 08544 Email address: seri@@math.princeton.edu and Igor Rodnianski Address: Department of Mathematics, Princeton University, Princeton NJ 08544 Email address: irod@@math.princeton.edu
Abstract.

This is the first in a series of papers in which we initiate the study of very rough solutions to the initial value problem for the Einstein vacuum equations expressed relative to wave coordinates. By very rough we mean solutions which cannot be constructed by the classical techniques of energy estimates and Sobolev inequalities. Following [Kl-Ro] we develop new analytic methods based on Strichartz type inequalities which results in a gain of half a derivative relative to the classical result. Our methods blend paradifferential techniques with a geometric approach to the derivation of decay estimates. The latter allows us to take full advantage of the specific structure of the Einstein equations.

1991 Mathematics Subject Classification
35J10

The following local existence and uniqueness result (well posedness) is well known (see [H-K-M] and the previous result of Ch. Bruhat [Br] for s≥4s\geq 4.)

Theorem 1.1.

Considered the reduced equation (3) subject to the initial conditions (4) and (5) for some s>5/2s>5/2. Then there exists a time interval [0,T][0,T] and unique( Lorentz metric) solution 𝐠∈C0​([0,T]×ℝ3){\bf g}\in C^{0}([0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3}), ∂𝐠μ​ν∈C0​([0,T],Hs−1)\partial{\bf g}_{\mu\nu}\in C^{0}([0,T];H^{s-1}) with TT depending only on the size of the norm ‖∂𝐠μ​ν​(0)‖Hs−1\|\partial{\bf g}_{\mu\nu}(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}. In addition condition (5) remains true on any spacelike hypersurface Σt\Sigma_{t}, i.e. any level hypersurface of the time function t=x0t=x^{0}.

We establish a significant improvement of this result bearing on the issue of minimal regularity of the initial conditions:

Main Theorem Consider a classical solution of the equations (3) for which (1) also holds11 1 In other words for any solution of the reduced equations (3) whose initial data satisfy the constraint equations, see [Br] or [H-K-M]. The fact that our solutions verify (1) plays a fundamental role in our analysis.. We show22 2 We assume however that TT stays sufficiently small, e.g. T≤1T\leq 1. This a purely technical assumption which one should be able to remove. that the time TT of existence depends in fact only on the size of the norm ‖∂𝐠μ​ν​(0)‖Hs−1\|\partial{\bf g}_{\mu\nu}(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}, for any fixed s>2s>2.

Remark 1.2.

Theorem 1.1 implies the classical local existence result of [H-K-M] for asymptotically flat initial data sets Σ,g,k\Sigma,g,k with ∇g,k∈Hs−1​(Σ)\nabla g,k\in H^{s-1}(\Sigma) and s>52s>\frac{5}{2}, relative to a fixed system of coordinates. Uniqueness can be proved for additional regularity s>1+52s>1+\frac{5}{2}. We recall that an initial data set (Σ,g,k)(\Sigma,g,k) consists of a three dimensional complete Riemannian manifold (Σ,g)(\Sigma,g), a 2-covariant symmetric tensor kk on Σ\Sigma verifying the constraint equations:

∇jki​j−∇itr​k=0\nabla^{j}k_{ij}-\nabla_{i}\,\mbox{tr}k=0
R−|k|2+(tr​k)2=0R-|k|^{2}+(\mbox{tr}k)^{2}=0

where ∇\nabla is the covariant derivative, RR the scalar curvature of (Σ,g)(\Sigma,g). An initial data set is said to be asymptotically flat (AF) if there exists a system of coordinates (x1,x2,x3)(x^{1},x^{2},x^{3}) defined in a neighborhood of infinity33 3 We assume, for simplicity, that Σ\Sigma has only one end. A neighborhood of infinity means the complement of a sufficiently large compact set on Σ\Sigma. on Σ\Sigma relative to which the metric gg approaches the Euclidean metric and kk approaches zero44 4 Because of the constraint equations the asymptotic behavior cannot be arbitrarily prescribed. A precise definition of asymptotic flatness has to involve the ADM mass of (Σ,g)(\Sigma,g). Taking the mass into account we write gi​j=(1+2​Mr)​δi​j+o⁡(r−1)g_{ij}=(1+\frac{2M}{r})\delta_{ij}+o(r^{-1}) as r=(x1)2+(x2)2+(x3)2r=\sqrt{(x^{1})^{2}+(x^{2})^{2}+(x_{3})^{2}} →∞\rightarrow\infty. . According to the positive mass theorem M≥0M\geq 0 and M=0M=0 implies that the initial data set is flat. Because of the mass term we cannot assume that g−e∈L2​(Σ)g-e\in L^{2}(\Sigma), with ee the 33D Euclidean metric.

Remark 1.3.

The Main Theorem ought to imply existence and uniqueness55 5 Properly speaking uniqueness holds, with s>2s>2, only for the reduced equations. Uniqueness for the actual Einstein equations requires one more derivative, see [H-K-M]. for initial conditions with HsH^{s}, s>2s>2, regularity. To achieve this we only need to approximate a given HsH^{s} initial data set( i.e. ∇g∈Hs−1​(Σ),k∈Hs−1​(Σ)\nabla g\in H^{s-1}(\Sigma),k\in H^{s-1}(\Sigma), s>2s>2 ) for the Einstein vacuum equations by classical initial data sets, i.e. Hs′H^{s^{\prime}} data sets with s′>52s^{\prime}>\frac{5}{2}, for which theorem 1.1 holds. The Main Theorem allows us to pass to the limit and derive existence of solutions for the given, rough, initial data set. We don’t know however if such an approximation result for the constraint equations exists in the literature.

For convenience we shall also write the reduced equations (3) in the form

(6) 𝐠α​β​∂α∂βϕ=N⁡(ϕ,∂ϕ){\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}\phi=N(\phi,\partial\phi)

where ϕ=(𝐠μ​ν)\phi=({\bf g}_{\mu\nu}), N=Nμ​νN=N_{\mu\nu} and 𝐠α​β=𝐠α​β​(ϕ){\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}={\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}(\phi).

Expressed relative to the wave coordinates xαx^{\alpha} the spacetime metric 𝐠{\bf g} takes the form:

(7) 𝐠=−𝐧2​d​t2+gi​j​(d​xi+𝐯i​d​t)​(d​xj+𝐯j​d​t){\bf g}=-{\bf n}^{2}dt^{2}+g_{ij}(dx^{i}+{\bf v}^{i}dt)(dx^{j}+{\bf v}^{j}dt)

where gi​jg_{ij} is a Riemannian metric on the slices Σt\Sigma_{t}, given by the level hypersurfaces of the time function t=x0t=x^{0}, 𝐧{\bf n} is the lapse function of the time foliation, and 𝐯{\bf v} is a vector-valued shift function. The components of the inverse metric 𝐠α​β{\bf g}^{\alpha\beta} can be found as follows:

𝐠00=−𝐧−2,𝐠0​i=𝐧−2​𝐯i,𝐠i​j=gi​j−𝐧−2​𝐯i​𝐯j.{\bf g}^{00}=-{\bf n}^{-2},\quad{\bf g}^{0i}={\bf n}^{-2}{\bf v}^{i},\quad{\bf g}^{ij}=g^{ij}-{\bf n}^{-2}{\bf v}^{i}{\bf v}^{j}.

In view of the Lorentzian character of 𝐠{\bf g} and the spacelike character of the hypersurfaces Σt\Sigma_{t},

(8) c​|ξ|2≤𝐠i​j​ξi​ξj≤c−1​|ξ|2,c≤𝐧2−|𝐯|g2c|\xi|^{2}\leq{\bf g}_{ij}\xi^{i}\xi^{j}\leq c^{-1}|\xi|^{2},\qquad c\leq{\bf n}^{2}-|{\bf v}|_{g}^{2}

for some c>0c>0.

The classical local existence result for systems of wave equations of type (6) is based on energy estimates and the standard Hs⊂L∞H^{s}\subset L^{\infty} Sobolev inequality. Indeed using energy estimates and simple commutation inequalities one can show that,

(9) ‖∂ϕ⁡(t)‖Hs−1≤E​‖∂ϕ⁡(0)‖Hs−1\|\partial\phi(t)\|_{H^{s-1}}\leq E\|\partial\phi(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}

with a constant EE,

(10) E=exp⁡(C​∫0t‖∂ϕ⁡(τ)‖Lx∞​𝑑τ)E=\exp\bigg(C\int_{0}^{t}\|\partial\phi(\tau)\|_{L_{x}^{\infty}}d\tau\bigg)

By the classical Sobolev inequality,

E≤exp⁡(C​t​sup0≤τ≤t‖∂ϕ⁡(τ)‖Hs−1​d​τ)E\leq\exp\bigg(Ct\sup_{0\leq\tau\leq t}\|\partial\phi(\tau)\|_{H^{s-1}}d\tau\bigg)

provided that s>52s>\frac{5}{2}. The classical local existence result follows by combining this last estimate, for a small time interval, with the energy estimates (9).

This scheme is very wasteful. To do better one would like to take advantage of the mixed Lt1​Lx∞L_{t}^{1}L_{x}^{\infty} norm appearing on the right hand side of (10). Unfortunately there are no good estimates for such norms even when ϕ\phi is simply a solution of the standard wave equation

(11) □​ϕ=0\square\phi=0

in Minkowski space. There exist however improved regularity estimates for solutions of (11) in the mixed Lt2​Lx∞L_{t}^{2}L_{x}^{\infty} norm . More precisely, if ϕ\phi is a solution of (11) and ϵ>0\epsilon>0 arbitrarily small,

(12) ‖∂ϕ‖Lt2​Lx∞​([0,T]×ℝ3)≤C​Tϵ​‖∂ϕ⁡(0)‖H1+ϵ.\|\partial\phi\|_{L_{t}^{2}L_{x}^{\infty}([0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3})}\leq CT^{\epsilon}\|\partial\phi(0)\|_{H^{1+\epsilon}}.

Based on this fact it was reasonable to hope that one can improve the Sobolev exponent in the classical local existence theorem from s>52s>\frac{5}{2} to s>2s>2. This can be easily done for solutions of semilinear equations, see [Po-Si]. In the quasilinear case, however, the situation is far more difficult. One can no longer rely on the Strichartz inequality (12) for the flat D’Alembertian in (11); we need instead its extension to the operator 𝐠α​β∂α∂β{\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta} appearing in (6). Moreover, since the metric 𝐠α​β{\bf g}^{\alpha\beta} depends on the solution ϕ\phi, it can have only as much regularity as ϕ\phi itself. This means that we have to confront the issue of proving Strichartz estimates for wave operators gα​β∂α∂βg^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta} with very rough coefficients 𝐠α​β{\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}. This issue was recently addressed in the pioneering works of Smith[Sm], Bahouri-Chemin [Ba-Ch1], [Ba-Ch2] and Tataru [Ta1], [Ta2], we refer to the introduction in [Kl1] and [Kl-Ro] for a more thorough discussion of their important contributions.

The results of Bahouri-Chemin and Tataru are based on establishing a Strichartz type inequality, with a loss, for wave operators with very rough coefficients66 6 The derivatives of the coefficients 𝐠{\bf g} are required to be bounded in Lt∞​Hxs−1L_{t}^{\infty}H_{x}^{s-1} and Lt2​Lx∞L_{t}^{2}L_{x}^{\infty} norms, with ss compatible with the regularity required on the right hand side of the Strichartz inequality one wants to prove. . The optimal result77 7 Recently Smith-Tataru [Sm-Ta] have shown that the result of Tataru is indeed sharp. in this regard, due to Tataru, see [Ta2], requires a loss of σ=16\sigma=\frac{1}{6}. This leads to a proof of local well posedness for systems of type (6) with s>2+16s>2+\frac{1}{6}.

To do better than that one needs to take into account the nonlinear structure of the equations. In [Kl-Ro] we were able to improve the result of Tataru by taking into account not only the expected regularity properties of the coefficients gα​βg^{\alpha\beta} in (6) but also the fact that they are themselves solutions to a similar system of equations. This allowed us to improve the exponent ss, needed in the proof of well posedness of equations of type88 8 The result in [Kl-Ro] applies to general equations of type (6) not necessarily tied to (1). In [Kl-Ro] we have also made the simplifying assumptions 𝐧=1{\bf n}=1 and 𝐯=0{\bf v}=0. (6), to s>2+2−32s>2+\frac{2-\sqrt{3}}{2}. Our approach was based on a combination of the paradifferential calculus ideas, initiated in [Ba-Ch1] and [Ta2], with a geometric treatment of the actual equations introduced in [Kl1]. The main improvement was due to a gain of conormal differentiability for solutions to the Eikonal equations

(13) Hα​β​∂αu​∂βu=0H^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}u\partial_{\beta}u=0

where the background metric HH is a properly microlocalized and rescaled version of the metric 𝐠α​β{\bf g}^{\alpha\beta} in (6). That gain could be traced down to the fact that a certain component of the Ricci curvature of HH has a special form. More precisely denoting by L′L^{\prime} the null geodesic vectorfield associated to uu, L′=−Hα​β∂βu∂αL^{\prime}=-H^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\beta}u\partial_{\alpha}, and rescaling it in an appropriate fashion99 9 such <L,T>H=1<L,T>_{H}=1 with TT is the unit normal to the level hypersurfaces Σt\Sigma_{t} associated to the time function tt,, L=b​L′L=bL^{\prime}, we found that the 𝐑L​L={\bf R}_{LL}=Ric(H)​(L,L)(H)(L,L), verifies the remarkable identity:

(14) 𝐑L​L=L⁡(z)−12​Lμ​Lν​(Hα​β​∂α∂βHμ​ν)+e{\bf R}_{LL}=L(z)-\frac{1}{2}L^{\mu}L^{\nu}(H^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}H_{\mu\nu})+{\mbox{e}}

where z≤O⁡(|∂H|)z\leq O(|\partial H|) and e≤O⁡(|∂H|2)e\leq O(|\partial H|^{2}). Thus, apart from L⁡(z)L(z) which is to be integrated along the null geodesic flow generated by LL, the only terms which depend of the second derivatives of HH appear in Hα​β​∂α∂βHH^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}H and can therefore be eliminated with the help of the equations (6).

In this paper we develop the ideas of [Kl-Ro] further by taking full advantage of the Einstein equations (1) in wave coordinates (6). An important aspect of our analysis here is that the term L⁡(z)L(z) appearing on the right hand side of (14) vanishes identically. We make use of both the vanishing of the Ricci curvature of 𝐠{\bf g} and the wave coordinate condition (2). The other important new features are the use of energy estimates along the null hypersurfaces generated by the optical function uu and a more efficient use of the conormal properties of the null structure equations.

Our work is divided in three parts. In this paper we give all the details in the proof of the Main Theorem with the exception of those results which concern the asymptotic properties of the Ricci coefficients( the Asymptotics Theorem), the isoperimetric and trace inequalities on 2-surfaces. We give precise statements of these results in section 4. Our second paper [Kl-Ro2] is dedicated to the proof of the Asymptotics Theorem. The isoperimetric and trace inequalities together with some other results needed in [Kl-Ro2] are proved in our third paper [Kl-Ro3].

We strongly believe that the result of our main theorem is not sharp. The critical Sobolev exponent for the Einstein equations is sc=32s_{c}=\frac{3}{2}. A proof of well posedness for s=scs=s_{c} will provide a much stronger version of the global stability of Minkowski space than that of [Ch-Kl]. This is completely out of reach at the present time. A more reasonable goal, at the present time, is to prove the L2L^{2}- curvature conjecture, see [Kl2], corresponding to the exponent s=2s=2.

2. reduction to decay estimates

The proof of the main theorem can be reduced to a microlocal decay estimate. The reduction is standard1010 10 see [Kl-Ro] and the references therein; we quickly review here the main steps. The precise statements and their proofs are given in section 8.

    Energy estimates

    Assuming that ϕ\phi is a solution1111 11 i.e. a classical solution according to theorem 1.1. of (6) on [0,T]×ℝ3[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3} we have the apriori energy estimate:

    (15) ‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]∞​H˙s−1≤C​‖∂ϕ⁡(0)‖H˙s−1\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{\infty}_{[0,T]}\dot{H}^{s-1}}\leq C\|\partial\phi(0)\|_{\dot{H}^{s-1}}

    Strichartz estimate To prove our Main Theorem we need, in addition to (15) an estimate of the form:

    ‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]1​Lx∞≤C​‖∂ϕ⁡(0)‖Hs−1\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{1}_{[0,T]}L_{x}^{\infty}}\leq C\|\partial\phi(0)\|_{H^{s-1}}

    for any s>2s>2. We accomplish it by establishing a Strichartz type inequality of the form,

    (16) ‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]2​Lx∞≤C​‖∂ϕ⁡(0)‖H1+γ\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{2}_{[0,T]}L_{x}^{\infty}}\leq C\|\partial\phi(0)\|_{H^{1+\gamma}}

    (17) ‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]∞​H1+γ+‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]2​Lx∞≤B0,\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{\infty}_{[0,T]}H^{1+\gamma}}+\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{2}_{[0,T]}L^{\infty}_{x}}\leq B_{0},

    (18) ‖∂ϕ‖L[0,T]2​Lx∞≤C⁡(B0)​Tδ.\|\partial\phi\|_{L^{2}_{[0,T]}L^{\infty}_{x}}\leq C(B_{0})\,T^{\delta}.

    for some δ>0\delta>0. Thus, for sufficiently small T>0T>0, we find that (16) holds true.

Remark 2.2.

In view of the proof of the Main Theorem presented above, which relies on the final estimate (18), we can in what follows treat the bootstrap constant B0B_{0} as a universal constant and bury the dependence on it in the notation ≲\lesssim we introduce below.

Definition 2.3.

We use the notation A≲BA\lesssim B to express the inequality A≤C​BA\leq CB with a universal constant, which may depend on B0B_{0} and various other parameters depending only on B0B_{0} introduced in the proof.

The proof of theorem 21 relies on a generalized Morawetz type energy estimate which will be presented in the next section. We shall in fact construct a vectorfield, analogous to the Morawetz vectorfield in the Minkowski space, which depends heavily on the “background metric” H=H(λ)H=H_{(\lambda)}. In the next proposition we display most of the main properties of the metric HH which will be used in the following section.

8. Proof of the reduction steps

In this section we give precise statements and proofs for the reduction steps discussed in section 2. Recall the equation (3), written in the form (6),

(101) 𝐠α​β​∂α∂βϕ=N⁡(ϕ,∂ϕ){\bf g}^{\alpha\beta}\partial_{\alpha}\partial_{\beta}\phi=N(\phi,\partial\phi)

We consider solutions ϕ\phi of (101) such that the components of both ϕ\phi and ϕ−1\phi^{-1} are uniformly bounded. Moreover 𝐠μ​ν{\bf g}_{\mu\nu} approach the Minkowski metric 𝐦μ​ν{\bf m}_{\mu\nu} at infinity according to (5). To avoid repeating this statement in what follows we introduce the following notation:

8.21. Properties of the metric 𝐠<λ{\bf g}_{<\lambda}

Recall that 𝐠<λμ​ν=P≤2−M0​λ​(𝐠μ​ν){\bf g}^{\mu\nu}_{<\lambda}=P_{\leq 2^{-M_{0}}\lambda}({\bf g}^{\mu\nu}) where 𝐠μ​ν{\bf g}^{\mu\nu} is the inverse of the Lorentz metric 𝐠μ​ν=ϕ{\bf g}_{\mu\nu}=\phi. We shall use the notation 𝐠<λ{\bf g}_{<\lambda} to denote the inverse of 𝐠<λμ​ν{\bf g}^{\mu\nu}_{<\lambda}. Observe that, in view of our assumption λ≥Λ\lambda\geq\Lambda, 𝐠<λ{\bf g}_{<\lambda} defines a Lorentz metric in our spacetime region [0,T]×ℝ3[0,T]\times{\mathbb{R}}^{3}. It clearly depends on the solution ϕ\phi of the quasilinear problem (101). In the next proposition we state the properties of the family 𝐠<λ{\bf g}_{<\lambda} which follow from the bootstrap condition (108) on ϕ\phi. We denote by 𝐑α​β​(𝐠<λ){\bf R}_{\alpha\beta}({\bf g}_{<\lambda}) the components of Ricci curvature of the metric 𝐠<λ{\bf g}_{<\lambda}.

8.37. Commutator lemma

We conclude this section by presenting the proof of lemma 7.1 from section 21. Recall that the definition of the exterior region Ext t={u≤t/2}\mbox{Ext\,}_{t}=\{u\leq t/2\}.

Lemma 8.38.

Consider a vectorfield X=∑iXi∂iX=\sum_{i}X^{i}\partial_{i} vanishing on the complement of the exterior region Ext t\mbox{Ext\,}_{t} of Σt\Sigma_{t} and PP the standard Littlewood-Paley projection on frequencies of size 1. Then, for arbitrary scalar functions ff we have the inequality:

(169) ‖[P,X]​f‖L2​(Ext t)≲supi,j‖∂iXj‖L∞​(Ext t)​‖f‖L2​(Σt)\|[P,X]f\|_{L^{2}(\mbox{Ext\,}_{t})}\lesssim\sup_{i,j}\|\partial_{i}X^{j}\|_{L^{\infty}(\mbox{Ext\,}_{t})}\|f\|_{L^{2}(\Sigma_{t})}

Proof First observe, by expanding X=Xj∂jX=X^{j}\partial_{j} relative to our system of our coordinates on Σt\Sigma_{t}, that [P,X]=[P∂j,Xj]−P(∂jXj)[P,X]=[P\partial_{j},X^{j}]-P(\partial_{j}X^{j}). We shall denote Pj=P∂jP_{j}=P\partial_{j}, the modified cut-off of the unit frequencies. In what follows, the roles of PP and PjP_{j} are identical. The convolution kernels of P,PjP,P_{j} are represented by the smooth functions P​(x),Pj​(x)P(x),P_{j}(x) verifying the condition that |P⁡(x)|,|Pj​(x)|≲|x|−k|P(x)|,|P_{j}(x)|\lesssim|x|^{-k} for any k>0k>0 and |x|≥1|x|\geq 1. In particular, for any functions w,vw,v

v\displaystyle v =∫ΣtP⁡(x−y)​(w⁡(y)−w⁡(x))​v​(y)​𝑑y\displaystyle=\int_{\Sigma_{t}}P(x-y)\big(w(y)-w(x)\big)v(y)\,dy
=−∫01∫ΣtP(x−y)(x−y)i∂iw(τx+(1−τ)y)v(y)dydτ\displaystyle=-\int_{0}^{1}\int_{\Sigma_{t}}P(x-y)(x-y)^{i}\partial_{i}w(\tau x+(1-\tau)y)v(y)\,dy\,d\tau

As a consequence,

(170) ‖[P,w]​v‖L2​(Σt)≲‖∇w‖L∞​(Ext t)​‖v‖L2​(Σt)\|[P,w]v\|_{L^{2}(\Sigma_{t})}\lesssim\|\nabla w\|_{L^{\infty}(\mbox{Ext\,}_{t})}\|v\|_{L^{2}(\Sigma_{t})}

We shall show that

Since all XjX^{j} vanish outside of Ext t\mbox{Ext\,}_{t} and PP is a bounded operator on L2​(Σt)L^{2}(\Sigma_{t}), we can easily estimate the second term,
